articles.title: Always choose the good soap
articles.subtitle: (Angelo D’Amico/Shutterstock) I’ve been thinking about soap again. Back in February I wrote about an Apple-related revelation I had while washing my hands on vacation: We stayed at a nice hotel rather than the less-nice-but-cheaper VRBO condo rental we...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I’ve been thinking about soap again.

Back in February I wrote about an Apple-related revelation I had while washing my hands on vacation:

We stayed at a nice hotel rather than the less-nice-but-cheaper VRBO condo rental we usually do. Because I’m me, I started thinking about Apple. Like Apple, the nice hotel’s brand promise is that it’s a nice hotel.

If the hotel didn’t clean its rooms well, didn’t provide soap that smelled nice, didn’t maintain the in-room refrigerator, didn’t clean the swimming pool, it would probably decrease its expenses and increase its profit margin. But over time, it would lose its niceness and become a lousy, overpriced hotel.

Earlier this month, John Gruber wrote about how he hopes incoming Apple CEO John Ternus can perform a bit of a reset on Apple’s advertising strategy. In recent months Apple has announced that it’s adding ads to Apple Maps, and ( as John has documented ) it’s allowed incredibly low-quality, scammy ads to infest Apple News.

While Apple can spin adding ads to Apple Maps as a revolutionary new way for businesses to be discovered, it’s telling that its initial announcement was hidden inside a press release about an entirely different product, and introduced as “Enhanced Discoverability in Apple Maps.

” Those choices show that this isn’t something Apple is actually proud of—and that the people in charge of communicating and explaining Apple’s decisions to the world are at odds with those who are making the decisions about expanding revenue.

Apple also recently expanded App Store ads, creating more clutter at the top of App Store search results. It similarly pitched this as an opportunity for developers—but of course, it’s really an opportunity for developers to take a portion of the money they make from the App Store after Apple’s cut and hand it right back to Apple so that their apps don’t become invisible. What a racket.

But Apple’s approach to grinding out additional revenue doesn’t stop with advertising. The recent release of Apple Creator Studio should’ve been a highlight, because it groups a bunch of useful creative apps in one place for a reasonable price. Instead, its launch was marred by the inclusion of Apple’s free productivity apps in the bundle, requiring users to download new versions and (at least initially) display aggressive subscription promotions in the Numbers, Pages, and Keynote interface.

To this day, you’re confronted with an ad for Creator Studio every time you create a new document in those apps, and their default toolbars contain buttons that won’t work unless you subscribe to the bundle.

As a result, Apple has essentially turned its free productivity suite—software that was designed to enhance the inherent value of Apple’s products—into a freemium package with upsell to a creative professional subscription bundle that’s irrelevant (and a terrible value! ) for most of its existing users.

There are many more examples. Using notifications to promote subscriptions and badging the Settings app to push AppleCare plans are among the ways Apple has chosen to intervene in the user experience to drive revenue.

I’m actually not opposed to the idea that Apple should communicate opportunities for its customers to get more out of their devices—but it should be careful not to cross the line into actively annoying those customers. If someone doesn’t want to see what you offer, you need to accept that and go away—not keep needling them. Apple often falls on the wrong side of that line.

Which brings me back to the hotel soap.

Apple’s most valuable asset is its brand. Not its real estate, not its intellectual property, not even any particular product. Even the mighty iPhone has no value if, over time, the traits that differentiate it from competitor products are erased. Apple’s brand has always stood for higher quality products—you pay more, but you get more. Apple has never wanted to be the low-price leader.

It didn’t put stickers on the first Intel Macs to get some marketing dollars from Intel. It doesn’t load up new Macs with loads of lousy bundled third-party software like so many PCs do.

Those are choices Apple has made that cost the company revenue, but they’ve got a bigger purpose. They reinforce the brand.

Opting not to add more revenue to the bottom line is a difficult choice for anyone working at a profit-driven corporation. I used to be in that position at my former employer, defending the overall product against a constant stream of advertising and biz-dev deal proposals that would add incremental revenue. Believe me, arguing to corporate executives that we should leave money on the table is a deeply uncomfortable role to take on—but it’s vital if you care about the bigger picture.

articles.title: Pastebot 3 Doubles Down on Mac Clipboard Automation and Introduces Two New Business Models
articles.subtitle: Pastebot’s Quick Menu. Tapbots has released Pastebot 3, a ground-up rewrite of the Mac clipboard manager that includes several powerful automation and customization options, along with two new pricing models.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Pastebot’s Quick Menu.

Tapbots has released Pastebot 3, a ground-up rewrite of the Mac clipboard manager that includes several powerful automation and customization options, along with two new pricing models.

Pastebot was already one of the Mac’s best clipboard utilities, capable of managing an extensive collection of copied text and images in multiple formats, PDFs, URLs, files, and HTML, along with metadata. The app can handle up to 1,500 clippings and features fast search, extensive customizable keyboard shortcuts, list and detail views of clipboard items, and iCloud sync between multiple Macs.

Pastebot 3’s main menu.

What sets Pastebot 3 apart is its addition of deep automation tools. Not only does the update add MCP support, making it an excellent tool to use with Claude or ChatGPT/Codex, but it includes a brand new CLI that you or an agent can use from Terminal or incorporate into scripts you build. Commands include:

List available Pastebins

Browse and search clipboard history

Filter results by Pastebin or date

Retrieve the full text of a clipping

Retrieve images from clippings

List available Pastebot filters

Apply filters to clippings or supplied text

Place an existing clipping on the clipboard

Create new text or image clippings

Paste clipboard contents into the frontmost app

Delete individual clippings

articles.title: AAPL stock rallies 15% as investors favor AI caution and welcome price increases
articles.subtitle: Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.

While we disagreed with that analysis, investors do now seem to be welcoming the company’s caution when it comes to AI spending, with the stock rallying 15% since that June low …

The company’s shares slid 4% the day after the keynote, but there were a number of macroeconomic factors affecting a wide range of stocks at the same time, including US strikes against Iran after the downing of an American helicopter.

The stock has rallied even more substantially since then, pushing it back into record territory. Bloomberg believes that AI is a factor in this, albeit somewhat indirectly. It suggests that investors are growing increasingly skeptical about AI spending by other companies and says that Apple’s more cautious approach is now seen as a positive.

The stock’s reversal reflects rising unease about the prospects for heavy spending on AI paying off, with Apple’s decision not to participate in the data center arms race increasingly being viewed as an asset, rather than a liability, even though its AI offerings have repeatedly frustrated investors.

“There’s a battle in the market, and right now Apple is benefiting because it isn’t in the storm that the rest of the AI trade is in,” said Mark Bronzo, chief investment strategist at Rye Strategic Partners. “People are concerned about what kind of return hyperscalers could get from their AI spending [and] as a result, investors have gravitated back to Apple as a steady-eddy name without those risks. ”

Louis Navellier, chief investment officer at Navellier & Associates [said] “Pricing for the folding phone will be so strong that it will offset the memory issue on margins, and I think demand will be so strong that it will really support growth.”

articles.title: Twisted Wonderland, which envisions Disney villains as hot anime boys, returning later this year
articles.subtitle: Twisted Wonderland's anime will be back soon, catboys included Related While Kingdom Hearts probably still takes the cake for the strangest Disney tie-in, Twisted Wonderland, a gacha game that reimagines Disney characters as hot anime boys, certainly comes...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Twisted Wonderland's anime will be back soon, catboys included

Related

While Kingdom Hearts probably still takes the cake for the strangest Disney tie-in, Twisted Wonderland, a gacha game that reimagines Disney characters as hot anime boys, certainly comes pretty close. The series’ anime adaptation is getting a second season, and Disney Japan just revealed that it’s streaming exclusively on Disney Plus this December.

The upcoming season will be centered on the Savanaclaw dorm, which is styled after Scar from The Lion King. That means there will be a lot of catboys this time around. For those unfamiliar with this series, Disney Twisted Wonderland is a mobile game set at Night Raven College, a school where each dorm is themed after a different Disney villain.

However, instead of a single anime boy directly representing a bad guy, each of the dorms is vaguely based on a villain. For instance, there are multiple heartthrobs styled around The Little Mermaid ’s Ursula. Black Butler creator Yana Toboso was heavily involved with the game, and he designed its characters and wrote its script.

The first season of the anime debuted last year with eight episodes and centered on the Heartslabyul Dorm (based on Alice in Wonderland ’s Queen of Hearts). The show is planned for three seasons. The game also has an ongoing manga adaptation.

As for season two of the anime, Takahiro Natori is returning to direct and handle series composition. Shin Kataga will co-direct. Yoichi Kato is the main writer, while Haruka Nakana and Akane Sato are adapting Toboso’s character designs. The show will once again be animated by Yumeta Company and Graphinica.

The series follows Yuuken Enma, a boy who finds himself summoned to another world through a magic mirror (yes, this is an isekai ). He gets to know the school’s top students while looking for a way home. The gacha game the show is based on has proven massively successful, generating over $715 million since its release in 2020. It has been downloaded over 6 million times worldwide.

Hasbro and Fathom Entertainment are bringing the original 1986 animated film The Transformers: The Movie back to the big screen this fall. The movie will receive a limited theatrical run in 4K resolution starting on September 17 to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the franchise. Fans can look forward to seeing the beloved characters return to cinemas across the United States with some entirely new surprises waiting at the end.

A brand new post credits scene awaits longtime returning fans

During a recent panel at San Diego Comic-Con, Hasbro revealed that this release will feature an exclusive addition. For the first time ever, audiences will get to see a brand new post credits cinematic chapter of the story. This extra scene was created specifically for the upcoming theatrical event to give both new and returning viewers a fresh reason to experience the classic story in a crowded room.

The studio is using this anniversary event as part of a year long apology tour campaign. The creators want to acknowledge the massive heartbreak fans felt decades ago when the movie famously killed off Optimus Prime. The return to theaters gives everyone a chance to relive the action and finally heal from that shocking cinematic moment together.

The theatrical run includes exclusive merchandise and premium format options

Tickets for the 40th anniversary screenings will officially go on sale online and at local theater box offices on August 7. The limited cinema experience will run through September 21 in the United States and the United Kingdom, with other international locations joining in on the exact same dates. For those wanting a more immersive watch, the film will also play in the premium 4DX format.

Fans heading to the theaters can also grab exclusive collectible items while supplies last. Participating locations will sell specially designed popcorn buckets and unique drinkware to mark the anniversary. Between the updated 4K visuals, the fresh story content, and the physical collectibles, this fall event aims to be a definitive celebration for anyone who grew up watching the iconic robot factions battle it out.

articles.title: I’m disappointed Apple will charge for AI security camera features in the Home app
articles.subtitle: iOS 27 One of the things tucked away in the small print of macOS 27 beta 3 is the news that you’ll need a 2TB iCloud+ subscription in order to use the new AI features for home security cameras in the Apple Home app.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
iOS 27

One of the things tucked away in the small print of macOS 27 beta 3 is the news that you’ll need a 2TB iCloud+ subscription in order to use the new AI features for home security cameras in the Apple Home app.

While some are suggesting that we shouldn’t be too surprised by this, I do find it a somewhat disappointing move by Apple …

Apple announced significant AI-powered upgrades to the Home app at this year’s WWDC.

Intelligent Home app notifications

One of these was using Apple Intelligence to replace a whole sequence of individual security notifications with a single summary. At present, something as routine as a family member arriving home might generate a notification that they were seen in the driveway, then that the garage door was opened, then that the garage door was closed, then that they were seen at the front door, then that the front door was unlocked, and finally that it was locked.

In iOS 27, all of those individual notifications are replaced with a single one saying that the family member arrived home.

Three AI features for video footage

But the bigger improvements was an upgrade of HomeKit Secure Video from 1080p to 4K, and the use of Apple intelligence to analyze footage from home security cameras. Apple highlighted three intelligent capabilities.

With generated video descriptions, users can quickly understand what happened across a sequence of video clips, even without watching them. They can also search through camera clips so they can easily find what they’re looking for, like a package delivery. At the top of the Search page, the Home app elevates noteworthy clips that users may want to review, so they can quickly see important moments.

Macworld spotted an important note in the release notes for the latest developer beta.

articles.title: Unlock or recover your Mac using a special boot volume
articles.subtitle: Several years ago, Apple began hiding disk partitions and volumes on the startup drive. The first was a secret volume with a tiny operating system on it that would let you boot from it, after which you could restore from a Time Machine backup, run First Aid...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Several years ago, Apple began hiding disk partitions and volumes on the startup drive. The first was a secret volume with a tiny operating system on it that would let you boot from it, after which you could restore from a Time Machine backup, run First Aid in Disk Utility, or reinstall Mac OS X or macOS. Over the years, Apple has multiplied those hidden locations and added more sophistication to what they offer.

These boot volumes are:

recoveryOS: The current name and form of the special volume described above, which boots into the Recovery Assistant “app. ” You can run Disk Utility (and First Aid), reinstall macOS, launch Safari to access Apple Support pages, modify startup security settings (rarely required these days), and access Terminal. With Terminal, you can reset your macOS password.

If your Mac can’t start up properly, it will try to launch the Recovery process within recoveryOS, which performs automatic repairs that Apple doesn’t document. If successful, you can then restart into macOS.

Fallback recoveryOS: If recoveryOS is damaged—and that can happen—you can press the power button twice, quickly, and then keep holding it the second time. This fallback recovery volume can’t change startup security, but it can help you diagnose what’s going on. This is the duct-tape belt that helps if your pants come unbuttoned (macOS won’t boot) and your suspenders break (regular recoveryOS fails).

Repair Assistant: From a powered-down state, press the power button until you hear the startup chime, then press and hold Command-D. (On an Intel Mac, hold the D key at startup. ) The Diagnostics app can run hardware tests that might help narrow down a problem before you bring in Apple Support, or they may ask you to boot into that mode and share the results of the tests they have you run.

Repair Assistant can fail, too, if its volume is damaged. You may then have to perform a special “ revive or restore ” operation, which requires another Mac. Or you may need a full reinstall using a bootable macOS installer.

macOS: macOS is a sort of hidden boot volume for the last several releases. You don’t boot from the system; instead, a read-only snapshot of the system is mounted, and then booted from. This is part of Apple making system resources immutable through cryptography and at startup.

Besides using recoveryOS for the above tasks, you might also need to use it to unlock your Mac after locking it in Find My and to reset your password using a FileVault Recovery Key. Here’s how.

Unlock your Mac

While it’s not a common scenario, it could happen to you: you accidentally leave your Mac somewhere, or it’s stolen. Thinking quickly, you launch Find My on another of your devices or go to iCloud. com/find and log in. You then tap or click a few buttons to lock your Mac. If the Mac is connected to the Internet, it restarts and locks immediately.

(Despite promising to display the message you entered when you locked it, macOS does not do so. ) If it’s not connected, it restarts the next time it has Internet access.

The account used to lock the Mac is the only one that can unlock it, and you must be in front of the Mac to perform that operation. Apple limits each Mac to having Find My enabled from a single account. Here are the steps:

When you see the macOS Recovery title, click the account profile below it. Enter the account’s password and click Continue.

If you entered it correctly, “Authentication succeeded” appears. Click Restart.

The Mac restarts and shows Activate Mac after it boots up. This time, all the active macOS accounts are shown. Click one, and then enter its password. Click Next.

You now can choose to either use your Apple Account or a macOS password to continue. If you opt for the Apple Account, enter the full address or phone number as shown. Then enter the account’s password. Otherwise, you can click to enter the Mac password, which Apple says is the last one used to unlock the Mac in a regular session before it was locked.

If you’re the only user on the Mac, that’s easy to figure out. (In testing with Golden Gate public beta 2, I wasn’t able to get the Mac password option to work, and I’ve had it fail in Tahoe, too. ) Sometimes neither works. Choose Restart from the Apple menu in that case and try again.

articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Claude Code has a new simulator button.

Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.

The process of setting up a simulator is simple. A new button with an iPhone icon appears when you open an existing project. Click it and a new iPhone simulator pane opens to the right by default. However, clicking on the name of the simulator reveals a list of every available simulator. You can also run multiple simulators at once, but that immediately made my aging M1 Max Mac Studio start to chug a little.

With access to your running app, Claude Code is more effective at debugging UI bugs.

Once you have the simulators that you want open, simply ask Claude Code to run and test your app, and it gets to work, building the app, installing it in the simulator, opening it, and poking around. I loaded up a simple word game I’ve been playing with, and after a few minutes, Claude Code found a UI bug while controlling the simulator. I asked it to fix the issue, which it did, then tested and committed. My testing has been limited, but so far it looks like a simple, effective loop.

It’s also worth noting that Claude Code is running the simulator directly inside the Claude app. This is not computer use, meaning windows aren’t going to be opening and getting in your way as you work on something else. All in all, the addition of the simulator, like the inclusion of an in-app sandboxed browser a couple of weeks ago, is a great update to Claude Code.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: The MacStories Public Beta Preview
articles.subtitle: The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.

It’s not my final take on Golden Gate by any means; after all, I’ve only been using it for about a month, and there will be several more turns in the beta cycle between now and the public release. However, I’ve used Golden Gate long enough to help you make an informed decision about whether or not to install the public beta now.

Of course, it’s impossible for me to account for everyone’s unique Mac setups when considering Golden Gate’s stability, but it’s worth reiterating what I’ve said in past previews: modern Apple betas have been consistently stable. That’s to say, the risks of using the public beta are modest. It’s been years since I’ve had a critical app fail or lost data.

I never go into beta season without a backup plan, though. If something goes terribly wrong, I have backups, backups of those backups, and alternate Macs I can switch to in the event of a disaster. I don’t expect to have to go to Plan B, but if you’re going to jump on the Beta Bus, you should have a Plan B, too.

Okay, you’ve been warned. Let’s get to the fun part.

Supported By

Inoreader

Every year’s macOS update is a little different, but Golden Gate is more different than most. Instead of focusing on tentpole features and apps (with the exception of a new Siri app), macOS 27’s updates fall into three broad categories:

refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design language,

hundreds of system-level changes intended to improve your Mac’s performance, and

Apple Intelligence, which includes the new Siri app as well as many other AI additions to existing system apps.

It’s been a while since the “Snow Leopard Moment.”

With so many past macOS updates focusing on system apps, it’s refreshing to see Apple take a more holistic system-level approach, which harkens back to how most people remember OS X Snow Leopard. In fact, during WWDC briefings, Apple representatives likened the Golden Gate update to Snow Leopard before anyone in the room even asked about it.

Snow Leopard is remembered as a release that focused on performance over features. The reality is that the update also introduced its fair share of new features, but many were less splashy from a user-facing standpoint. They were under-the-hood updates that made the Mac work better without users having to think about it much. In that sense, Golden Gate has a lot in common with Snow Leopard.

Other than the brand new Siri app, you probably won’t notice that much is different when you first launch the new version. But over time, the changes will reveal themselves, adding up to a whole that – with few exceptions – is greater than the parts.

So let’s take a closer look at how Liquid Glass has evolved, the most significant system changes, and what it’s like to use Siri and other Apple Intelligence updates in Golden Gate’s public beta.

Design

Windows stand out from each other more, and the sidebar runs edge to edge in Golden Gate.

When Fable 5 returned last week, I knew exactly what to throw at it. In February, I started a project out of frustration that likewise ended in frustration, so I put it on the shelf and waited. Five months later, Fable 5 was released, and I knew it was time to finish Editor, a single-view diffing tool for writers rather than developers.

At MacStories, we all write in Markdown, and we’ve used GitHub to share and sync changes among team members since 2015. GitHub is primarily a developer tool, but it’s a fast, reliable way to share our Markdown-formatted article files, too.

We use GitHub the most for the Club MacStories newsletters. Every week, Federico, Devon, Jonathan, and I work on sections for MacStories Weekly and save them to a GitHub repo. That allows any of us to sync the sections locally for reading, editing, and assembling the issue.

The trouble is that as great as Markdown text editors are to write and GitHub is for versioning and syncing, there isn’t a good way to view the changes someone has made to a document. I know because I’ve been looking for a solution for a long time. Some Markdown apps like iA Writer and Bear support versioning or backups, but I’ve yet to find a text editor that can visualize changes made by someone else based on a document’s Git history.

Of course, developers have many ways to track changes to code, including GitHub Desktop, Kaleidoscope, and Git Tower. Code is just text, so those apps can be used by writers, too. However, the process of writing and editing prose is fundamentally different from code. I’ve tried the apps above and others, and it’s just too hard to track changes in the formats development tools use.

This is what it’s like trying to track changes in GitHub Desktop.

We wouldn’t have stuck with GitHub as long as we have if it didn’t work, but that hasn’t made the friction of reviewing changes any less frustrating, especially on Fridays when we send MacStories Weekly. That’s when I had the idea for Editor. I was trying to parse some changes Devon had made to one of my stories with GitHub Desktop, and the friction finally got to me.

One obvious problem was the side-by-side document view many code diffing tools use. I wanted more detail than most diffing tools offer, but in a single, readable view, so I could skim through changes quickly.

Most agent-assisted projects benefit from some up-front research and planning. I knew what I wanted would sink or swim on the design, not the app’s underlying Markdown viewer, so I spent time researching systems for visualizing document edits.

That’s when I came across Upwelling, a multi-author project from Ink & Switch that describes itself as “an independent research lab exploring the future of tools for thought.” In their research paper, the authors described my exact problem:

Unfortunately, version control tools like Git, which are designed for software development, do not suit the needs of writers. Git cannot compare or merge files from WYSIWYG editors such as Microsoft Word… and graphical user interfaces for Git are cluttered with complex concepts such as commit hashes and visualizations of non-linear branching and merging histories.

Ink & Switch’s solution, a prototype collaborative text editor, wasn’t what I wanted to build, but the research behind it was full of interesting ideas that helped me settle on several principles for what would become Editor:

Document changes needed to be visible in a single view that carefully balanced highlighting changes with readability;

A writer should be able to instantly switch from the marked-up version of their document to the clean original and edited final version;

Changes needed to be categorized by filterable types like punctuation, word choice, capitalization, insertions, and deletions to reduce clutter in heavily edited documents;

Change types would be color coded using a side rail system inspired by maps of London’s tube system;

Navigating among individual edits needed to be done by simple j/k keyboard input; and

Global document navigation should employ a mini-map of a document’s edit regions (a feature borrowed from developer IDEs like Xcode) to make it easy to jump from one area of a document to another.

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: That evil Car Park Capital tycoon game is only getting more evil with MicroProse as publisher, but it still looks gorgeous
articles.subtitle: New additions include riot police and nuisance parking Car Park Capital is a triumphantly unwholesome tycoon game in which you try to make an entire society utterly dependent on cars.
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
New additions include riot police and nuisance parking

Car Park Capital is a triumphantly unwholesome tycoon game in which you try to make an entire society utterly dependent on cars. You start with a relatively green-ish map, and do your best to tarmac it all over. A strange and unlikely prospect, I know!

When we first covered this motorist management sim last year, the options included putting up billboards to brainwash obstinate pedestrians, and selling people banana-mobiles. Since then, developer Hilko Janssen of Hilkojj Interactive has found a publisher in MicroProse. If you were hoping that MicroProse might persuade Janssen to give up on his visions of total automotive apocalypse, you were hoping in vain.

Car Park Capital has oil derricks now. It has offensively jaunty golf carts, for people who can't even be bothered to walk to the other end of a parking lot. It has leaking fuel trucks, and giant plastic trees to replace all the vegetation you've murdered with those leaking fuel trucks. It has riot police to beat up all the people protesting about habitat loss.

Here are some highlights from Janssen's social media and Steam devlogs. Firstly, you'll be able to build a network of drive-thru facilities - giant toilets, giant perfume dispensers, giant hamburger stands, giant Ferris Wheels – the better to ensure that people never have to leave their vehicles. To operate your fast food joints you'll of course need a beef industry, with giant sausage machines. If your cows escape, you can send flying saucers to abduct them.

Yes, this is the cartoonish kind of evil. See also: you can build carparks inside the Pyramids of Giza. But it's a proper management simulation, nonetheless, and there's a core of seriousness. One of the early sparks for Car Park Capital was an old piece of real-life American car propaganda, Give Yourself The Green Light.

"Car dependency is a lot lesser here in the Netherlands than in the United States but it wasn’t always like this," Janssen explained to Parking Reform in June. "In the 60s and 70s car dependency was in fact on the rise here too. Where I live there were plans to fill in Amsterdam’s canals with concrete to make roads and highways.

"That never happened here thankfully but it did in a nearby city only to turn it back into a canal decades later," he continued, "so it went from water to highway and back to water. Living in a place where you can see both what was lost and what was recovered definitely plays into the way I think about making this game."

Some more highlights from that interview: NPCs are capable of parking badly, wasting a space. "I might also add other little annoyances, like someone parking in a place that blocks an important road, or someone endlessly circling a full parking lot and complaining," Janssen said. "I think these little details help capture the absurdity of car dependency, making the game more relatable and humorous."

The goal of enforcing car use obliges a different spin on certain city management fundamentals. You'll want to demolish those inner city apartment blocks and replace them with pricey suburban homes, for example, so that people have to drive to work.

The greatest horror is that Car Park Capital still looks gorgeous, with dorky isometric citizens and toytown buildings that remind me of 1997's comparably villainous Constructor (though the more immediate visual inspiration is RollerCoaster Tycoon ). I absolutely can't wait to build a Cadillac carousel in every nature reserve and ruin the air quality for miles around.

articles.title: Best Thunderbolt and USB-C docking stations for your MacBook 2026
articles.subtitle: Macworld Plug your MacBook in and out of a multi-port laptop docking station to swiftly add multiple devices and external displays with just one cable connection to your laptop.
articles.author: Macworld
articles.content:
Plug your MacBook in and out of a multi-port laptop docking station to swiftly add multiple devices and external displays with just one cable connection to your laptop. We tested the top contenders to find the best Thunderbolt and USB-C docks available to owners of the MacBook Air and MacBook Pro. MacBook Neo users can use any of these docks but are limited to a 10Gbps bandwidth and some display limitations.

Thunderbolt, USB4 or USB-C

The connectors all look the same (technically known as a “Type-C connector”), but there are significant differences, particularly on speed that will determine both data-transfer rate and higher external display refresh rates.

USB-C: 5Gbps or 10Gbps

USB4: 20Gbps or 40Gbps

Thunderbolt 3 and 4: 40Gbps

Thunderbolt 5: 80Gbps / 120Gbps

Our list Which ports does my MacBook have will show you how many USB-C or more likely one of Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5 that you have.

While a Thunderbolt 4 (TB4) dock will be enough for most casual users, if you can stretch the budget go for a TB5 dock as it will remain current for years, saving you money in the long term, and is backwards compatible with earlier versions and all the way back to USB-C. High-end professionals should always aim for Thunderbolt 5.

The dock needs one (“ upstream “) Thunderbolt or USB-C port for connecting to and charging your laptop (although all recent MacBooks can also power via the MagSafe 3 port), and at least another (“ downstream “) to attach further devices (hard drives, external display, and others).

The USB-C MacBook Neo has just the one data port, with the other reserved for charging. A dock with Power Delivery will greatly expand the entry-level Mac laptop.

For more detail, read our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 vs USB4 explainer.

Add external displays to your MacBook

If you use your laptop as your principal computer, attaching at least one larger display to create a hybrid desktop/laptop setup, with a keyboard and mouse, will boost your productivity. You can turn that 13in MacBook’s cramped screen real-estate into an iconic iMac-sized 27in or even larger screen by adding an extra display—or connect two or even four large monitors to extend your screen across your whole desk.

Take a look at our recommended best monitors and displays for Mac and also the best portable monitors for Mac.

You’ll get two or more Extended mode screens (where the screen extends beyond what you can see on the laptop screen) using a Thunderbolt connection (or DisplayPort/HDMI).

Natively over mere USB-C, Macs can connect to only one external display in Extended mode, as opposed to Mirrored mode (which replicates exactly what you get on the laptop screen) but DisplayLink is third-party software that allows some docks to extend to up to four screens on even the most basic Mac.

DisplayLink-supporting docks are also the only way that non-Pro/Max M1 and M2 MacBooks can connect more than one external display.

articles.title: Review: Xteink X3 is the little e-reader the world’s not quite ready for
articles.subtitle: An e-reader magneted to the back of a smartphone, just as the prophecy foretold. The market for small e-readers has been booming lately.
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
The market for small e-readers has been booming lately. Earlier this year, Jason took a look at the Xteink X4, a pint-sized reading device that was about as light and small as they come. But those maniacs at Xteink weren’t done yet: they followed it up with the $79 X3, which is unbelievably even lighter and smaller.

I wouldn’t blame you for wondering if there’s such a thing as too small and light—at 3.84 inches by 2.51 inches (and just 0.2 inches thick) the X3 is still larger than, say, a credit card, but not by much. The screen itself measures just 3.7 inches, more than half an inch smaller than the X4’s 4.3 inch, but its 259 ppi resolution still makes it plenty easy to read on. 1 At that size it’s little imposition to take it with you wherever you go. Easy to lose? Maybe. Easy to love? Yes.

For one thing, this small size unlocks at least one capability that the X4 couldn’t fully deliver upon—the ability to stick to the back of your phone. Like the X4, the X3 has a MagSafe-compatible magnet in its rear case and it fits just about perfectly on the back of my iPhone 17 Pro, nestled below the camera plateau.

However, the magnet is not particularly strong, and it lacks the secondary stabilizing magnet that you see on official MagSafe accessories, meaning it wobbles around a bit. I wouldn’t call it a super secure connection, but it’s pretty good if you’re just slipping it in and out of a pocket. Just be aware that it probably will come loose.

Like the X4 before it, the X3 features a pair of rocker switches on the front for a total of four possible buttons. But they’ve opted to skip the X4’s side mounted rocker switch in favor of a single buttons on each side. There’s also an on/off switch at the top (plus a recessed button used for resetting the device). And with all of that, they somehow managed to continue to fit a microSD slot in the top. The bottom left corner also has a little set of holes for a lanyard or wrist strap.

The one casualty of the smaller X3, however, is the port. The X4 was big enough to accommodate a USB-C connector, but the X3’s thin profile makes that impossible. Instead, there’s a pogo-pin USB cable that connects to four magnetic contacts on the reader. Is this a step back? Strictly speaking, yes.

Using a proprietary connector is a bummer in the year 2026, especially because it means having to keep track of a single-use cable. That said, once you get the X3 up and running, the only real need for the connector is charging, and the battery on this thing lasts a very long time. (I’ve yet to run it down in several weeks of usage.

) Just remember to make a note of where you stow that cable for the point months down the road when you do need to charge it and find yourself wondering whatever happened to it.

As with the X4, the X3 lacks any sort of screen lighting, meaning that it’s strictly a “read in bright light” device. But don’t worry, because Xteink has already unveiled a new X4 Pro with the company’s first lit screen. 2

All in all, I found the X3 very comfortable to read on, whether attached to my iPhone or not. The side buttons work great as page-turners, and the screen is high-contrast and sharp enough to make text render very clearly. All in all, it’s a great reading experience—if you take into account one major caveat.

Soft where?

The elephant in the room for the Xteink X3 is the software. Xteink ships the X3 with its own built-in firmware which, by all accounts, has improved since the first version. But I can’t really tell you, because upon opening the box and powering up the device, the first thing I did was install Crosspoint, the open-source community-built firmware that has turned this device from a curiosity into a real contender. 3

Unlike a lot of other firmware replacements, Crosspoint is super easy to install; you can do it right from a web browser. While it’s not fully free of technological hurdles, I’d say that most people comfortable using an e-reader or updating their iPhones will be able to handle the process with few problems. And the benefits are manifold.

Crosspoint goes beyond simply turning this into a functional device and into one that is actually fun to use. It’s got a straightforward, easy to navigate interface that makes it simple to do everything from reading to loading books (accomplished via a web-based interface). For those who like to tweak their reading setup, there are plenty of configuration options, everything from screen orientation to hyphenation and, yes, custom fonts loaded via the SD card.

Even the onscreen keyboard that you need to use for various configuration tasks is pretty solid for what’s available—on par with navigating via an onscreen keyboard with a game controller, in my opinion. I wouldn’t want to have to type in my Wi-Fi password every time—and you don’t, because it saves it for you—but one time was fine.

There are also a bunch of other features that might appeal to those who want to take reading to the next level. For example, support for Open Publication Distribution System (OPDS) standard means that if you want to host your book library on your own server, you can point your reader at that and download any of the books you already own directly to your device. There’s also support for KOreader sync to help keep your place between supported devices. 4

Crosspoint has been so successful, in fact, that the team at Xteink has smartened up and started collaborating. (This after a brief moment when it looked like the company might try to firmware lock its devices.

) Now, not only do the “developer editions” sold directly by the company continue to allow you to install the custom firmware, the company has been working with the Crosspoint team to make sure new devices, like the X4 Pro, will already be supported when they arrive. While Xteink hasn’t quite adopted Crosspoint as the default OS, it’s not far off.

articles.title: Snazzy Labs Puts the Mac’s Upcoming Game Porting Toolkit 4 Through Its Paces
articles.subtitle: Over at Snazzy Labs, Quinn Nelson has a great in-depth look at the changes coming to Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit with macOS 27 this fall. Paired with Metal 4, it’s a real leap over what’s possible today, and Nelson showcases the difference well.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Over at Snazzy Labs, Quinn Nelson has a great in-depth look at the changes coming to Apple’s Game Porting Toolkit with macOS 27 this fall. Paired with Metal 4, it’s a real leap over what’s possible today, and Nelson showcases the difference well.

Thanks to the upcoming update, Nelson was able to use CrossOver, a Windows-to-Mac compatibility layer that allows PC games to be played on a Mac, to spotlight some impressive numbers on games ranging from Red Dead Redemption to the recently released 007 First Light.

Not all games Nelson tried showed the same leap in performance, but that’s true on compatibility layers like Proton on the Steam Deck, too. What’s remarkable is that it’s all done in software and as Nelson points out, the advent of coding agents like Codex and Claude may help bring more PC games to Mac using the Game Porting Toolkit by reducing the porting costs.

Nelson also makes a pitch for an Apple gaming device. I agree with him that more than ever, the pieces, right down to a hardware-focused incoming CEO, are all there for such a device, and I remain optimistic. However, I’ve made the case for such a device for years now to no avail. Still, whether or not Apple builds gaming hardware itself, watch the full video above. It’s a fantastic view of how far the Mac has come as a potential gaming platform since the advent of Apple silicon.

I really enjoyed this explanation from Federighi about Apple’s approach to AI and why he thinks it’s totally reasonable that some people are spooked by how fast things are moving right now:

And while I think we can look at this as yet another thing of the scale of the Industrial Revolution, which changed our world in a giant way, that displaced a lot of people in the process and still occurred over like 80 years. And now this is happening in a compressed time frame. And so I think it’s fair for people to say, “Wow, I’m not quite certain what this is going to mean for me.

I've been watching Colorfire's cat-themed Meow product line with much interest over the years. While I've already got a kitty-eared headset, I'm sure a full feline-themed set-up would help me achieve my final form as a hardware writer. The Meow series' ME26A PC case may prove the perfect canvas towards realising that dream.

In terms of styling, the ME26A is low-key compared to other entries in the Meow series. For starters, pizza-eating mascot Bobi is seemingly nowhere to be seen (unlike the Meow-X gaming PC set Colorfire showed off at last year's Computex ). There's a very fun 'Meow'-shaped air grate on the front, and even a bit of tasteful wooden trim. The cat hasn't completely left the build, though.

The ME26A PC case also enjoys an almost subtle kitty paw motif, with orange decals on the chassis itself, just above the front I/O panel. Daubed in kitty pawprints, the front I/O features 1x USB-A, plus 1x USB-C port rated for up to 20 Gbps.

It also happens to feature one of the best power buttons I've ever seen—if I can start my day by squishing fake toe beans, I know it's going to be a good day (via VideoCardz ).

Honestly, I already can't imagine a better thing to play Cat Mail Co. on, but let's talk case specs. Supporting both microATX and Mini-ITX motherboards, a cute, smaller form factor build is what the ME26A PC case aims for. That said, this case still supports standard-sized ATX power supplies, too. As for your all-important GPU, this case offers up to 435 mm of clearance—which is more than enough space for the Meow series' bright orange, twin-fan RTX 5050.

To keep everything cool, there's room for nine fans plus a 360 mm, top-mounted liquid cooler. Better yet, you won't be crying like a cat at dinner time trying to get inside the case to install these; the ME26A's dust filter and side panels can be popped off without the use of tools.

To burst my own bubble, though, Colorfire has not yet announced pricing information or region availability. Alas, my feline-themed build may be a dream I simply have to resign to the great cat bed in the sky.

This strategy tries to bypass older internet laws that usually protect social platforms from being responsible for what their users say, focusing instead on how the software is built and designed.

Families sue platforms for bad design instead of published content

For years, a rule known as Section 230 has protected internet companies from being treated as the publishers of user posts. If someone posts something harmful, the person is liable, not the platform. Pixelmator Pro now integrates more deeply with Creator Studio’s other apps. Final Cut Camera for the iPhone and iPad has been updated with support for Clean HDMI Out, more flexible ProRes support, and disabling of digital zoom. Motion now supports vector graphics, and Compressor gains Vision Pro features, while Freeform gains shape creation, opening images in Pixelmator Pro, a Dark Mode, folders, and drawing on the Mac. Plus, Pages, Keynote, and Numbers each added a handful of new features.

Creator Studio debuted just six months ago, so it’s good to see it already being updated with meaningful features. Creator Studio costs $12.99/month or $129/year. More information is available in Apple’s press release here.

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

articles.content:
The makers of the popular trading card game set want to address resale issues as well as violent incidents

Related

There's no end in sight to the pandemonium surrounding the Pokémon trading card game, where a single boxed product can be resold for hundreds if not thousands of dollars. The hobby has proven so profitable that people line up outside stores days ahead of a new release. Trading card robberies are a weekly occurrence.

For a family-friendly corporation like The Pokémon Company, this heightened state of affairs is horrible PR. To combat this dilemma, the makers of the Pokémon TCG are adopting increasingly strict measures meant to curb resale vultures.

Earlier this year, The Pokémon Company began requiring customers in Japan to provide government-issued ID before purchasing trading cards at official outlets. The system has not left Japan's shores, but it also does not appear to be a temporary experiment.

More recently, The Pokémon Company announced that five pop-up shops in Japan would soon begin using facial recognition technology for customers of elementary-school age or older. The company states that facial recognition is meant to ensure customers cannot revisit stores or make additional purchases.

If the system determines the customer is trying to bend the rules, "entry will be denied to that person based on the system's judgment," the announcement reads. The new system will be employed for the Japanese release of the Rayquaza-themed Storm Emeralda set that will be simultaneously released on Pokémon TCG Pocket.

Customers who refuse this type of surveillance will not be allowed to enter the stores at all. Trading card fans can leave the store and reenter by necessity — like, for example, to use the bathroom — but store employees must be informed first. Younger children will still be allowed into the store, but only under guardian supervision. The facial data will promptly be deleted "after a certain period of time."

The Pokémon Company's wider privacy policy states that the company can collect data that is not limited to facial recognition. That data includes photographs, audio recordings, digital media, email addresses, school names, occupations, workplaces, driver's license numbers, passport numbers, residence‑registration numbers and more.

This data is used for a number of reasons, from processing payments to developing market research. The collected information could theoretically be used in efforts against scalpers, but the policy does not explicitly state such a purpose.

Beyond ensuring a better customer experience, these efforts are being undertaken to maintain what the company calls "safety management." In March, a Pokémon Center store was closed after an employee was killed onsite by an alleged stalker. That store, the Pokémon Center Mega Tokyo, will officially reopen in August, The Pokémon Company announced Monday.

There's no indication that facial recognition or government ID requirements will be tested outside of Japan, but some fans may welcome such measures. Cards in the United States have become absurdly expensive, and — more importantly — their high value has sparked a wave of violent incidents.

articles.title: When Find My doesn’t help with separation anxiety
articles.subtitle: I dispense what might be called valuable insight to my friends, as well as in this public forum. My friends know the danger: they might become the topic of a column, which is true for my buddy Jeff, who left a bag containing his passport behind at a hotel.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
I dispense what might be called valuable insight to my friends, as well as in this public forum. My friends know the danger: they might become the topic of a column, which is true for my buddy Jeff, who left a bag containing his passport behind at a hotel. Fortunately, he had an AirTag in his bag. That was, however, just the beginning of the journey. (Jeff gave me permission to share his story.) 1

To avoid suspense, I’ll tell you that Jeff doesn’t have his bag back, but will soon.

Grate news

Jeff was out of town on business for a few days—he’s one of those nearly extinct creatures called a “ full-time technology reporter “—and was carrying his passport to Texas not because it’s another country (it hasn’t seceded yet), but because he lacks a Real ID-upgraded driver’s license.

He had a small bag with a few items, including the passport and an AirTag, that he didn’t need to carry, so he used the hotel safe. There have been many articles written about how unsafe hotel safes are, but it feels as if you’re in a decent hotel, it’s still another bar for someone to get through to steal your stuff.

Leaving in a bit of a rush, Jeff didn’t retrieve the bag from the safe. When he realized it wasn’t with him, thousands of miles later, he was peeved. Shouldn’t the “left behind” feature in Find My have alerted him? Find My showed the bag’s location, however. For some reason, it appeared as if it were in the hotel parking lot. I catastrophized with him, assuming it was stolen. He called the hotel, which said it wasn’t in lost and found.

A staff member went out, looked in the parking lot, and said the rough location was a grate—perhaps the bag had been stolen and someone had found the AirTag and dropped it through the slats? Which would imply that a hotel employee or a thief had managed to get into Jeff’s room after he left, open the safe, leave the hotel, and rummage through the bag in the parking lot before absconding.

That wasn’t the case (or valise). The hotel called back the next day. The previous staffer didn’t know, for some reason, that valuable left-behind items were tagged and placed in a safe in the basement, presumably below or near the parking lot. His bag, containing his passport and other items, would be sent back to him.

Jeff’s experience reveals several aspects of the Find My tracking system that you can take advantage of in advance or use if you’ve lost something or left it behind.

Don’t leave me!

Every device and item you have can be set to alert you when you “leave it behind.” I believe this setting is enabled by default, though Apple’s documentation isn’t clear on this point. All of my devices and items have it enabled, and Jeff found it was turned on for all his gear. Here’s how to check:

In a native Find My app, select the device (like a Mac) or an item (an AirTag or other Find My network item) in the list of such things.

On an iPhone, iPad, or Apple Watch, the action sheet appears. On a Mac, click the info (i) icon next to the item’s name on the map. In the upcoming version 27 operating system releases on all platforms, tap or click the More (…) button that appears when you select the device from the list.

Tap or click Notify When Left Behind, which should already show On. (In the 27 releases, tap or click When Left Behind.)

If disabled, turn it on.

Here’s a crucial detail: examine the “Notify me, except at” list. You can manually add to this set of locations (tap or click New Location). However, it primarily grows when you’re notified by an item or device being left behind, and then you tap or click in the notification to ignore it at that location. You are presented with the option to just exclude that item or device from that location or all of your equipment.

It’s very easy to approve that exclude-all button. (Jeff did not; his list didn’t include the hotel.) This can be convenient when you’re at a hotel, a friend’s house, or another location for a few days or frequently, and sometimes leave Find My-tracked stuff there. But once you ignore the location, you won’t get notified in the future. You can modify the list by hand, too.

Jeff may instead have been tripped up by the safe acting as a Faraday cage—a metal mesh or box that shields electromagnetic signals from passing through. The AirTag and other Find My items use Bluetooth to broadcast a rotating identifier at regular intervals. 2 If the safe blocked that signal, Jeff’s iPhone lost contact with the AirTag the moment the bag went in—a few days before he left.

articles.title: Nintendo Of America’s Original Pokémon Pitch From E3 1998 Is Wild To Watch Nearly 30 Years Later
articles.subtitle: Pokémon It’s always fascinating to see how differently the Pokémon series has presented itself over the years. The 30-year-old franchise has lived through multiple handheld and console generations, decades of anime, and its trading cards going from...
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Pokémon

It’s always fascinating to see how differently the Pokémon series has presented itself over the years. The 30-year-old franchise has lived through multiple handheld and console generations, decades of anime, and its trading cards going from potentially being “worth something someday” to being a treasure trove preyed upon by scalpers.

But before Pokémania became a worldwide phenomenon in the ‘90s, it had to get packaged and pitched to an audience outside of Japan. A video of the original E3 1998 showcase reel for Pokémon has been archived by the Video Game History Foundation, and this time capsule offers a wild look back on both Pokémon as a series, and also E3 and video game trade shows of the era.

While E3 is no more, the show was once the cornerstone of video game marketing every summer, with folks tuning in to watch press conferences where the execs of PlayStation, Nintendo, Xbox, and other companies showed trailers and demos for their upcoming games.

Though many likely remember E3 for these press conferences replete with flashy stages and celebrity appearances, at one point the show was much more subdued and directed more at retailers and businesses than anything else.

In 1998, Pokémon had already blown up in Japan and was on its way to English-speaking territories, so Nintendo brought a video showcasing the video games, anime, card game, and merchandise to the show.

The presentation is a bit jarring because it’s so clinical. It spouts off sales and anime viewership numbers, which were definitely impressive at the time considering the series was still only in Japan.

Still, hearing suits talk about how “Pokeymon” is a “phenomenal product” as they try to pitch retailers on how big of a hit they have on their hands offers a pretty clear demonstration of how E3 shifted over the years.

Though the show obviously remained useful as a place where companies could pitch their games and hardware to retailers, the messaging became much more player-focused over the years, with developers showing off games and trying to sell their games to an audience, rather than specifically to people who needed reassurance that a particular game would be worth putting on their shelves.

You’ll find little mention of Pokémon ’s belief in the power of friendship here, just a lot of numbers and statistics, and a disembodied voice saying they’re getting “reports” of known features of the Pokémon games instead of just saying “you’ll have to trade Pokémon with other players to complete the Pokédex. ”

It kinda gives me the ick, but one interesting thing in all this corporate speak is that you can hear an earlier version of the Pokémon anime theme song that included a different tagline than the one the show eventually settled on. While most people know the phrase “Gotta catch ‘em all! ” from the theme song, the version we hear in this video had different lyrics: “Catch ‘em if you can!

” This E3 took place in May 1998, a little under four months before the series would make its proper United States debut in September, so at some point the show re-recorded the theme song featuring Jason Paige that most folks know today.

Nowadays, Pokémon needs no introduction, nor does it need to tout sales numbers so Walmart will stock Red and Blue, but it is interesting to look back at relics of the ‘90s before Pikachu became a household name.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

White-hat hacker BobDaHacker revealed in a July 24 blog post (via The Register ) that "The Pope's official app exposes 700,000+ user emails." The vulnerability has since been fixed, but it seems only after BobDaHacker went public with their investigation—inquiries made by the hacker and by journalists stretching back to January this year went unanswered.

The vulnerability itself was pretty simple. When you sign up for Click To Pray, the site hands your user account an ID number. The first guy to sign up was one, the next was two, and so on, all the way into the hundreds of thousands.

Problem is, by visiting https://api.clicktopray.org/user/users/[ID number goes here], you could retrieve the name and email address, plus some other info, for whoever had the ID number you inputted. "No authorization check. No ownership validation. Just increment the number and get someone else's data. The Lord provides," writes BobDaHacker.

"Email address. First name. Last name. Country. Date of birth (or as their backend calls it, borned_date, because apparently bad grammar isn't a sacrament). Role. Whether the account has been deleted. All of it, for any user, no questions asked," they continue. "The response headers also have X-Powered-By: Express because the Vatican is running its prayer infrastructure on the framework you learn in week two of a Node.js bootcamp." I'm not smart enough to understand that, but it sounds witheringly funny.

articles.title: Apple Responds to Lawsuit Over Fake Bitcoin Wallet Scam in App Store
articles.subtitle: Apple is facing a new lawsuit from three customers who allegedly lost a combined $1.8 million after falling victim to a fake Bitcoin wallet app in the App Store, according to a complaint filed in California federal court on Friday.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple is facing a new lawsuit from three customers who allegedly lost a combined $1.8 million after falling victim to a fake Bitcoin wallet app in the App Store, according to a complaint filed in California federal court on Friday.

The complaint alleges that Apple violated California's Consumers Legal Remedies Act and other laws by failing to adequately review and monitor apps distributed through the App Store, despite marketing it as "a safe and trusted place to discover and download apps." Due to these assurances in Apple's marketing, the complaint said the plaintiffs trusted that a Sparrow Wallet app they downloaded from the App Store on iOS was legitimate, when in reality it was a fraudulent spoof designed to steal Bitcoin from users.

Sparrow Wallet is only available on Windows, macOS, and Linux. The popular Bitcoin wallet is not available on iOS, but scammers have released fake lookalike apps in the App Store that can trick users into giving up control of their funds.

"Users found their accounts had been wiped out and their cryptocurrency assets transferred to the scammers' private wallets," the complaint says. "This fraud succeeded precisely because Apple exploited the consumer trust it had deliberately cultivated through more than a decade of marketing the App Store as a uniquely safe and trusted environment."

The plaintiffs James Ramirez, Christopher Ellis, and Jalen Delgado had Bitcoin amounts that were worth approximately $875,000, $840,000, and $120,000 respectively stolen via the app from May to August of 2025, according to the complaint.

Even when victims reported fraud, the lawsuit alleges that Apple often took little to no action, and it says other fake Sparrow apps remain in the App Store.

Sparrow Wallet developer Craig Raw has publicly addressed Apple's slow response to multiple fake versions of his app appearing in the App Store. In a January 2024 social media post, for example, he said "there is still a scam 'Sparrow Wallet' app on the @Apple App Store, despite myself and others having reported it weeks ago."

Last month, Raw said his attempt at protecting users by submitting a "placeholder" app to the App Store that contained marketing screenshots stating that Sparrow Wallet is a desktop app only resulted in his Apple Developer account being flagged for termination due to "dishonest activity." Apple later reversed this decision.

The plaintiffs are seeking damages, including reimbursement of all funds wrongfully lost through the fraudulent Sparrow Wallet app.

Update — July 27 at 5:30 a.m. Pacific Time: In response to our request for comment, Apple said it has taken swift action to remove any apps impersonating Sparrow Wallet on the App Store and to terminate developer accounts associated with those apps.

Apple said developers who suspect that content available on an Apple service infringes on their intellectual property rights can submit a dispute form to Apple's legal department, and customers can report App Store scams or frauds too. Apple says it takes immediate action against apps that do not comply with its guidelines.

Apple previously announced that it terminated 193,000 developer accounts over fraud concerns and prevented over $2.2 billion in potentially fraudulent transactions in 2025.
